common_name: Yellow Crown Itoh Peony (Historic Semi-Double Yellow Intersectional Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Yellow Crown is one of the small original batch of intersectional hybrids raised by Toichi Ito in Japan from a cross of the herbaceous Paeonia lactiflora 'Kakoden' with the tree peony 'Alice Harding,' first flowering in 1964 and later registered in the United States by Louis Smirnow. Its semi-double, clear yellow flowers are marked with fine red flares near the center, carried on stems that reach deeply cut, tree-peony-like foliage well above most herbaceous peonies. Though it has since been eclipsed in popularity by later Itoh introductions such as Bartzella, it remains historically significant as one of the founding cultivars of the entire Itoh class, and like its relatives the top growth dies back fully to the ground each winter rather than persisting as a woody shrub. Plant in full sun with afternoon shade in hot climates, in deep, fertile, well-drained soil, and leave the crown undisturbed once established.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society), Paeonia Itoh Cultivars

common_name: Yellow Emperor Itoh Peony (Historic Ball-Form Yellow Intersectional Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Yellow Emperor shares the same parentage and origin as Yellow Crown, bred from Paeonia lactiflora 'Kakoden' crossed with the tree peony 'Alice Harding' in Toichi Ito's original intersectional breeding program and registered by Louis Smirnow in 1974. Its fragrant, ball-form flowers open a clear yellow, occasionally showing faint red blotching toward the center, on vigorous, well-branched stems backed by finely divided foliage inherited from its tree peony parent. As with other members of this founding Itoh group, the plant dies back completely to the ground in winter despite its shrub-like summer foliage, distinguishing it from true woody tree peonies. A white-flowered sport of this cultivar, discovered by Bill Seidl in Wisconsin in 1977, was later released as 'White Emperor.' Grow in full sun with afternoon shade in hot climates, in deep, fertile, well-drained soil, undisturbed once planted.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society), Paeonia Itoh Cultivars

common_name: White Emperor Itoh Peony (Rare White Semi-Double Intersectional Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: White Emperor arose as a chance white-flowered sport on Yellow Emperor, discovered by Wisconsin breeder Bill Seidl in 1977 and registered with the American Peony Society in 1989; truly white flowers remain rare within the Itoh class, making this an unusual and sought-after selection. Its semi-double blooms open crisp white with faint light-purple flares ringing the cream-colored stamens, held on the same strong, early-blooming stems and growth habit as its yellow parent. The dense, finely cut summer foliage carries the tree-peony look typical of intersectional hybrids, yet the entire plant collapses back to the ground with the first hard frosts, unlike a woody tree peony. Site it in full sun with afternoon shade in hot climates, in deep, fertile, well-drained soil, and avoid disturbing the crown once it is established.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society), Paeonia Itoh Cultivars

common_name: Viking Full Moon Itoh Peony (Single Light Yellow Intersectional Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Viking Full Moon was bred from a lactiflora crossed with a yellow-flowered tree peony hybrid by Pehrson and Seidl, first blooming in 1980-81 and registered with the American Peony Society in 1989. Its single flowers carry ten broad, overlapping light-yellow petals arranged in two flat rows around dull red flares that are largely hidden beneath a ring of yellow stamens, opening during the early herbaceous peony season. Strong stems hold the five- to six-inch blooms upright over mounded, deeply lobed foliage that shows its tree peony ancestry through summer before dying back completely at the first hard frosts. Grow in full sun with afternoon shade in hot climates, in deep, fertile, well-drained soil, and leave the clump undisturbed to build toward its fullest bloom.

common_name: Sonoma Amethyst Itoh Peony (Deep Lavender Semi-Double Intersectional Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Sonoma Amethyst was bred by California hybridizer Irene Tolomeo from an unnamed Paeonia lactiflora seedling crossed with the tree peony 'Golden Era,' and registered in 2001, giving the Itoh class one of its deepest lavender tones rather than the yellows and pinks that dominate the group. Its semi-double flowers open a rich, saturated amethyst-lavender over a lower, compact mound of dark, deeply cut foliage that carries the tree-peony look through the growing season. Despite the shrubby summer appearance, the entire plant dies back to the ground each winter in the manner of a herbaceous peony rather than persisting as woody growth. Plant in full sun with afternoon shade in hot climates, in deep, fertile, well-drained soil, and leave the crown undisturbed once it is sited.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society), Paeonia Itoh Cultivars

common_name: Berry Garcia Itoh Peony (Cream and Pink Semi-Double Intersectional Peony with Burgundy Flares)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Berry Garcia was bred by American hybridizer Don Smith from the lactiflora cultivar 'Martha W.' crossed with an unnamed Paeonia delavayi hybrid, first flowering in 2001. Its semi-double flowers open cream, flushed and edged in pink, with large burgundy flares marking the base of the petals around the central stamens, a color pattern distinct from the solid yellows and reds common among earlier Itoh introductions. The mounded plant holds its deeply cut, glossy foliage attractively through summer on sturdy stems that need no staking, then collapses back to the ground each winter as its herbaceous parentage takes over. Grow in full sun with afternoon shade in hot climates, in deep, fertile, well-drained soil, and leave the clump undisturbed to reach its fullest bloom over several seasons.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society), Paeonia Itoh Cultivars

common_name: Smith Family Yellow Itoh Peony (Fragrant Deep Yellow Semi-to-Fully-Double Intersectional Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Smith Family Yellow was introduced by American breeder Donald Smith in 2002, bearing very large, semi- to fully double flowers in a clear, deep yellow with golden stamens and a light fragrance that is more pronounced than in many other Itoh cultivars. The upright, midsized bush carries deep green, deeply lobed foliage reminiscent of its tree peony ancestry through the growing season, then dies back completely to ground level each winter in the manner of a herbaceous peony. It is a slow but steady grower that, once established, is notably resistant to deer and rabbit browsing compared with many garden perennials. Grow in full sun with afternoon shade in hot climates, in deep, fertile, well-drained soil, and leave the crown undisturbed once planted.
sources: Perennials.com Plant Profile, Paeonia 'Smith Family Yellow'
